newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Canadian commander holds talks with Zaire rebels.
newsitem.headline: Canadian commander holds talks with Zaire rebels.

text.p: Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, the Canadian commander of a proposed multinational intervention force for eastern Zaire, arrived in Goma on Thursday for talks with rebels who control much of the area.

A Reuters correspondent said Baril crossed the border from Rwanda in a three-vehicle convoy and went directly to the palace in Goma of Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, now in rebel hands. He declined to speak to journalists.
Officials of the United Nations UNHCR refugee agency will also be present at the talks with rebel Zairean leader Laurent Kabila.
Kabila, like his backers in neighbouring Rwanda, is against the presence of a multinational force in eastern Zaire on grounds that most Rwandan Hutu refugees had returned home.
The rebels control the eastern Zairean towns of Uvira, Kamanyola, Bukavu and Goma and say they plan to take their military campaign to the capital Kinshasa.
Canada, which is leading the UN-backed mission to help Rwandan and Burundi refugees in eastern Zaire, has suggested this week that air-drops of food could be made in the area.
The United States said on Wednesday it supported a Canadian proposal to set up a headquarters for an international force to ease the refugee crisis in Zaire.

The White House also said in a statement that it was putting personnel on alert, possibly to take part in airdrops of food to Rwandan refugees in Zaire but it said it had not made a final decision on whether to participate in the airdrops.
Canada, impatient with international indecision over the multilateral force approved by the United Nations on November 15, proposed on Tuesday that it be based at Entebbe, Uganda.

Western military leaders agreed in Stuttgart, Germany, last weekend, that the mission would be limited to delivering aid and bringing home the thousands of refugees, most of them Rwandans who fled civil war in their homeland in 1994.
Aid agencies have been unable to work properly in eastern Zaire since heavy fighting between Zairean rebels, Zairean government troops and Rwandan Hutu extremists flared up in October.

However, UNHCR spokesman in Goma Ray Wilkinson said air-drops should be a last resort, given the highly scattered refugee population. He told journalists they were "very expensive, and, in one of the most inhospitable parts of the world, will take a lengthy and major planning process".
U.S. air-drops to Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire during the 1994 crisis were widely regarded as a waste of time and resources.
